draft.title: Properties from bonding
card: Ionic
Strong attractions between oppositely charged ions hold the solid together. Ionic compounds have high melting points and are hard but brittle.
Conduction
Ionic compounds do not conduct as solids, because the ions are locked in place. They conduct when dissolved in water or melted, because the ions are then free to move.
Covalent

Many covalent substances are made of separate molecules. The attractions between molecules are weak and easy to overcome, so they often have low melting points. Molecules have no charged particles free to move, so they usually do not conduct.
Uses
Properties decide uses. Wax is a covalent substance that melts easily, so it suits candles. Salt, an ionic compound, has a high melting point and dissolves in water to conduct.
draft.remember: Ionic: high melting point, conducts only when dissolved or melted. Covalent molecules: often low melting point, usually no conduction.

a.q: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity, while a solution of it does?
opts: Its ions cannot move in the solid but can in solution
Its electrons cannot move in the solid but can in solution
Its molecules are packed close in solid, spread in solution
Its atoms have no charge in the solid but gain it in solution
a.why: Sodium chloride is made of ions. In the solid they cannot move, but in water they are free to move and carry charge. The option about electrons is tempting, but the charge carriers here are ions.
a.clue: What particles carry the charge, and can they move?

b.q: Sam tests two white solids. Solid X melts at 800 °C and its solution conducts. Solid Y melts at 60 °C and its solution does not conduct. What does this suggest about X and Y?
opts: X is ionic and Y is made of covalent molecules
X is made of covalent molecules and Y is ionic
Both X and Y are ionic compounds
Both X and Y are made of covalent molecules
b.why: A high melting point and a solution that conducts match an ionic compound. A low melting point and no conduction match covalent molecules. Reversing them is tempting if you think strong bonds mean low melting points, but strong attractions between ions need much more heat to break.
b.clue: Match each test result to ions or molecules.
